title: Adaptive connection handshake and graceful rollback for SDKs (Python/TS/Go)
creator: Ava Chen
description: PRD-level requirements for an adaptive connection handshake and graceful rollback mechanism that standardizes how Redwood SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go) negotiate streaming capabilities, backpressure semantics, pagination cursors, and safe rollback behavior across client and runtime versions. Goal is a single compatibility contract that minimizes client breakage when server-side capabilities change and makes downgrade/resume predictable for customers with long-lived streams.
scope: Define an explicit handshake protocol between SDK and Redwood runtime that advertises supported features: streaming modes (chunked vs evented), cursor formats, idempotency headers, backpressure windows, and retry semantics.
Specify client-side behavioral matrix for Python, TS, and Go SDKs when runtime responds with reduced capability (e.g., no streaming, truncated cursor format, reduced batch size).
Acceptance criteria and automated integration test harness (sdk-compat-suite) that runs cross-language scenarios including simulated network partitions and server capability downgrade.
Migration guidance and sample code for customers to opt into new handshake features while remaining compatible with older runtime versions.
out_of_scope: Runtime implementation details (ENG tickets will own kernel/runtime changes).
Telemetry schema overhaul — only minimal telemetry for compatibility decisions will be added.
Language-specific ergonomic reworks beyond the handshake surface (e.g., async API refactors) unless required for the contract.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Handshake: All three SDKs implement an HTTP/2 header-based handshake and WS fallback that includes: sdk-version, requested-features, preferred-stream-mode, and idempotency-capability. Test vectors exist in sdk-compat-suite.

2) Graceful downgrade: When server replies with a reduced feature set, SDKs must: emit a single telemetry event, translate streaming to polling/paginated fallback without data loss (when possible), and surface a single typed warning to application developers within one second of connection establishment.

3) Streaming resume: For long-lived streams, the handshake must negotiate a resume-token format. SDKs must be able to persist a resume token (opaque string) and resume within 30s of disconnection with at-most-once semantics for already-delivered units, documented per-language.

4) Pagination & cursors: Cursor format changes must be supported via versioned cursor namespaces. SDKs must detect unknown cursor namespaces and either attempt a server-side translation endpoint (if advertised) or fail with a deterministic error code and recovery steps.

5) Retry/backoff contract: SDKs implement a standard retry window algorithm: honor Retry-After and Retry-Quota headers, default to exponential backoff with jitter, and expose a hook for apps to override. End-to-end tests must validate behavior under 429/503 and partial stream failures.

6) Compatibility matrix: sdk-compat-suite must cover all permutations of (SDK version ±2, runtime version ±1) across streaming/pagination/retry features with pass/fail indicators. Tests run in CI against canary and stable runtime images.
7) Docs & migration: Publish PRD + short migration guide in Confluence and code snippets for each SDK. Docs must include a checklist for customers and staged rollout plan for the runtime change.
decisions: Use header-based capability negotiation as primary handshake; WS body-level negotiation only as fallback for older runtimes.
Resume tokens are opaque strings issued by the runtime; SDKs must persist them verbatim and not introspect format. Versioning is through namespacing in the token prefix.
Backpressure is modeled as a sliding window advertised by the runtime; clients must respect declared window sizes and pause reads when exhausted.
Fallback from streaming to paginated pulls is the preferred graceful-degrade path; clients should prefer this over dropping connections.
open_questions: Q1: Should the handshake include optional performance hints (e.g., preferred max-ttl for tokens)? Pros/cons and privacy implications need engineering input.
Q2: How should SDKs surface warnings for automatic fallbacks in log levels versus programmatic exceptions? Proposal: telemetry + opt-in exception raising hook.
Q3: Do we require server-side translation endpoints for old cursor formats, or should SDKs do client-side adapters? Cost estimates required from ENG.
